sm: Host Georgia Howe, filling in while John is out, opens the Tuesday, November 24th edition of Morning Wire. Former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang is returning after a break of a week and a half, and investors rallied at the news. The episode will ask what NVIDIA's comeback means for the AI industry. Also coming up, the Trump administration debuts a new transportation task force just in time for the holiday travel rush. And a new investigation into the world's most widely used herbicide may help explain the drop in testosterone among American men.

After a Chinese spy scandal rocked the stock market, Jensen Huang is resuming his role as NVIDIA's CEO. Guest Kyler Schmitz, a vice president at the data center company Patmos, says the board acted in shareholders' interest after the stock's nose dive. He reads the quick reinstatement as a sign that the damage to NVIDIA and to national security may have been overstated, especially after Huang testified to Congress. Schmitz says the concern was less about chip design leaking and more about illegal exports through intermediaries in Southeast Asia, allegedly tied to a foreign agent with whom Huang had an affair. He believes NVIDIA has a strong defense that it did not knowingly support such exports, though details are limited. On President Trump's role, Schmitz says Trump has been an advocate of Huang and put measured, positive pressure on the situation, but he thinks the board drove the decision. He calls NVIDIA a cornerstone of the AI industry, supplying chips and an ecosystem of software, and a champion of American open source AI, even as competitors emerge.

After a five-hour nationwide FAA ground stop last week, the Trump administration unveiled a plan to protect holiday travel. White House correspondent Mary Margaret Olohan explains that the so-called Tiger team includes officials from the FAA, the Department of Transportation, the Department of Defense, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. It met daily last week, ahead of the busiest travel week of the year. A White House spokeswoman said the FAA is examining near-term network configuration changes and ways to improve air traffic control stability by removing fragile components, while modernization continues. Olohan notes the administration has faced criticism over a lack of transparency, though many feel the crisis is being handled. Georgia then asks about ICE arrests at airports. Olohan describes the arrest of a father and daughter who overstayed their visas at Seattle's airport on November 21st as they boarded a domestic flight. The administration says it has expanded information sharing between TSA and ICE, and DHS called it targeted enforcement. Critics are unhappy, and Olohan expects more such arrests.

Federal health researchers have raised new concerns about glyphosate, the main ingredient in Roundup, and the Make America Healthy Again movement is calling it a win. Culture reporter Megan Basham explains that scientists at the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences released two reviews at the request of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. One found some evidence linking exposure to blood cancers such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and the other found tumors in mice and rats. These reviews are not peer reviewed, and Roundup's parent company noted the human results were mixed. They conflict with the EPA's long-held view that glyphosate is not likely carcinogenic. A separate peer-reviewed study of 55 animal studies linked glyphosate to lower sperm counts, abnormal sperm, and lower testosterone. The EPA is re-reviewing glyphosate after a 2022 court ruling, with HHS scientists involved, and expects an assessment early next year. Callie Means predicts a likely carcinogenic label, but the administration is divided, and farm groups say the evidence is not strong enough and that a ban would hurt American farmers.
